defender.name: De La Riva to Grasshopper Guard Defender
defender.description: How to stop the De La Riva inversion to Grasshopper Guard in BJJ. Recognition cues, back-take and pass options, and counters for the passing player.
defender.overview:
As the passing player facing a De La Riva hook, you are the defender when the bottom player tries to invert into Grasshopper Guard. The inversion is their response to your attempt to disengage - back-step, leg-drag, or circle - so the defensive battle is about denying them a clean roll, stripping their anchor before they commit, and recognizing that their rolling motion is itself an opportunity to take the back or finish a pass.

The critical window opens the instant the bottom player drops their head beneath your hip and starts to roll. Before that, strong base management and hook clearance prevent the inversion entirely. Once they commit, you have a choice: ride the roll to a back take while they are momentarily turned away, or step over and stack to flatten them before their hips elevate. The worst response is to chase the disengage carelessly and feed your weight into the very leg connection that powers their inversion.

Advanced defense centers on hook removal and back exposure. The De La Riva hook is their anchor; if you strip it before they roll, the inversion collapses back to upright guard. If they keep the hook and commit, ride their rotation and pursue the back rather than trying to out-muscle the leg entanglement they are building.
key_principles: Strip the De La Riva hook before you disengage - without the anchor the inversion cannot land cleanly
Recognize the head-drop beneath your hip as the commit signal for the inversion
Do not feed your weight into the hooked leg as you back-step; lighten and clear the leg instead
Their rolling motion exposes their back - ride the roll and hunt back control rather than resisting the leg
Stack and step over early to flatten them before their hips can elevate into the Grasshopper platform
Keep your free leg back and mobile so it cannot be threaded into a leg entanglement on the way down
Stay patient against a static De La Riva - only disengage on your terms, not theirs
recognition_cues: The bottom player keeps a live De La Riva hook on your near leg and grips your far leg or ankle even as you try to step away
The bottom player suddenly tucks their chin and drops their head down and underneath your near hip, looking back toward their own seat
The bottom player's shoulders settle to the mat and their hips begin to rotate upward as they initiate a granby-style roll under your base
You feel your near leg being followed and tethered through your back-step rather than coming free as expected

defensive_options.action: Strip the De La Riva hook by circling your knee out and clearing the foot before you disengage
defensive_options.when_to_use: Preventive - the moment you decide to back-step or circle away, before the bottom player drops their head to invert
defensive_options.if_successful: Without the hook the bottom player has no anchor; their inversion stalls and they are forced back to upright De La Riva while you continue your pass
defensive_options.risk: Reaching to clear the hook can momentarily lower your posture, giving them a window to off-balance you or attack the leg if you are slow

defensive_options.action: Ride the rolling motion and chase an inside hook to take the back
defensive_options.when_to_use: When the bottom player has already committed to the inversion and their back is momentarily turned toward you mid-roll
defensive_options.if_successful: You convert their committed inversion into a back take, arriving in back control as they expose their spine during the roll
defensive_options.risk: If you over-commit to the back before securing a hook, they can complete the inversion and entangle your chasing leg instead

defensive_options.action: Stack forward and step over to flatten them before their hips elevate
defensive_options.when_to_use: When you read the head-drop early and can drive forward before they surface from the roll
defensive_options.if_successful: Your forward pressure crushes the inversion before the Grasshopper platform forms, keeping them flattened and stalling their attack
defensive_options.risk: Driving forward feeds your weight toward their legs; if mistimed they redirect your pressure into an elevation sweep or inside ashi entry

defensive_options.action: Keep your free leg retracted and pommel it back as they reach to thread it
defensive_options.when_to_use: Throughout the disengage and roll, whenever the bottom player's legs seek your free leg for entanglement
defensive_options.if_successful: Denying the second leg connection prevents them from building a leg entanglement and keeps your passing options open as their inversion stalls
defensive_options.risk: Constantly retracting the leg can narrow your base and make you easier to off-balance if you neglect your overall posture

favorable_outcomes.how: When the bottom player commits to the inversion and turns their back during the granby roll, ride their rotation rather than fighting the leg. Chase an inside hook and chest connection as their spine exposes, arriving in back control as they roll under you.

Strip the De La Riva hook before disengaging and keep your free leg retracted. Without the anchor and without a second leg to thread, the inversion stalls and the bottom player is forced back to upright De La Riva, where you can continue your pass on your terms.

common_errors.error: Back-stepping while the De La Riva hook is still live
common_errors.consequence: The hook tethers your retreating leg and powers the inversion, so your disengage becomes the exact trigger that lands them in Grasshopper still connected to your base.
common_errors.correction: Strip or clear the hook first by circling your knee out and freeing the foot, then disengage. Never give up your angle while their anchor is still attached to your leg.

common_errors.error: Resisting the leg entanglement instead of recognizing the back-take opportunity
common_errors.consequence: By fighting their leg as they roll, you ignore that their back is exposed mid-inversion and miss the highest-percentage counter while they complete a leg attack.
common_errors.correction: When they commit to the roll, switch your intent from defending the leg to chasing the back - ride their rotation and secure an inside hook as their spine turns toward you.

common_errors.error: Driving forward heavily into the inversion without controlling the legs
common_errors.consequence: Your forward weight feeds directly into their elevation mechanics, letting them redirect your pressure into a sweep or inside ashi entry instead of being flattened.
common_errors.correction: Stack and step over only when you can do so before their hips elevate, and keep your free leg clear so your forward pressure does not become sweep fuel or an entanglement entry.

flashcards.question: Why is stripping the De La Riva hook the highest-priority defense against this inversion?
flashcards.answer: The De La Riva hook is the bottom player's anchor to your base. As long as it is live, your back-step or circle simply tethers your retreating leg and powers their roll, landing them in Grasshopper still connected to you. Clearing the hook before you disengage removes the anchor, so the inversion stalls and they are forced back to upright De La Riva.

trap: Retreat without clearing hook

flashcards.question: What opportunity does the bottom player's committed inversion create for you?
flashcards.answer: Their committed granby-roll turns their spine toward you, letting you ride the rotation into a back take. As they invert under your base their back is momentarily exposed, so rather than fighting the leg entanglement they are building, ride their rotation and chase an inside hook with chest connection, converting their committed inversion into back control.

trap: Chase the leg lock instead

flashcards.question: How can driving forward to flatten the inversion backfire, and how do you do it safely?
flashcards.answer: Driving forward feeds your weight into their legs, so flatten the inversion only early, before the Grasshopper platform forms. If mistimed, they redirect that forward pressure into an elevation sweep or an inside ashi entry rather than being flattened. Do it safely by stacking and stepping over only when you can beat their hips to the elevation, while keeping your free leg clear of their threading legs.

plausible: Stack hard the moment they invert
trap: Drive forward once platform's set

training_progressions.focus: Reading the inversion commit and stripping the hook before disengaging
training_progressions.description: Partner establishes De La Riva and telegraphs the inversion at 30-40% speed. Practice recognizing the head-drop cue and clearing the hook by circling your knee out before you back-step. 20-30 repetitions per session, both sides, prioritizing hook clearance over speed of pass.

training_progressions.focus: Converting a committed inversion into back control
training_progressions.description: Partner commits to the inversion at 50-60% intensity while you practice riding the roll and chasing an inside hook to take the back. 10-15 repetitions per session, developing the timing to follow their rotation rather than resisting their legs.

training_progressions.focus: Beating the hip elevation with forward pressure
training_progressions.description: Partner inverts and you practice stacking and stepping over early to flatten them before the Grasshopper platform forms, at 60-70% resistance. Emphasize keeping your free leg clear so your pressure does not feed a sweep. 10-15 reps per session.

training_progressions.focus: Full-resistance passing against an inverting De La Riva player
training_progressions.description: Start with the partner in De La Riva actively threatening the inversion to Grasshopper. Pass while choosing between hook clearance, back-take off the roll, and stack-and-flatten under competitive pressure. 5-minute rounds, multiple rounds per session.

variants_and_adaptations.variant_name: DLR to Grasshopper with Ankle Grip
variants_and_adaptations.description: Before inverting, the bottom player secures a grip on the opponent's far ankle as a second connection point. This reinforces the anchor so the roll is even less likely to spin out, and it pre-loads a straight ankle lock or inside ashi entry on surfacing.
variants_and_adaptations.when_to_use: When the opponent's far leg is reachable and you want maximum connection security through the roll, especially against athletic passers who clear hooks quickly

variants_and_adaptations.description: When the opponent circles toward the back side rather than the open side, switch from De La Riva to a Reverse De La Riva hook first, then invert from there into Grasshopper. The roll direction mirrors the standard entry to follow the opposite circle.
variants_and_adaptations.when_to_use: Against a passer who consistently circles to your back side to clear the standard De La Riva hook

variants_and_adaptations.description: Rather than settling the Grasshopper platform, the bottom player rolls straight through the inversion into a rolling kneebar on the hooked leg, using the momentum of the roll to load the submission as they surface.
variants_and_adaptations.when_to_use: When the opponent's near leg is extended and exposed during their back-step, making the kneebar available before they can square back up

source.position_integration: De La Riva to Grasshopper Guard is a connective transition that links the upright open-guard retention game to the inverted leg-attack game, making it a backbone of modern no-gi guard play. It sits in the same family as the Berimbolo and other De La Riva inversions, sharing the head-drop and shoulder-roll mechanics, but it surfaces in a leg-attack platform rather than a back-take spin. Strategically, it converts a passer's disengagement - the back-step, leg-drag, or circle that would normally beat a static guard - into an offensive opportunity, keeping the bottom player connected to the legs when an upright guard would have been passed. From Grasshopper, the transition feeds directly into inside and outside ashi-garami, kneebars, ankle locks, and elevation sweeps to X-Guard and Single Leg X-Guard, so it serves as the on-ramp to an entire leg-entanglement system. Mastering this inversion is essential for guard players who want their De La Riva to remain dangerous against passers who try to circle and disengage rather than pressure straight through, and it pairs with Reverse De La Riva recovery to cover both directions of escape.

source.name: Heel Hook from Grasshopper Guard
source.summary: The Heel Hook from Grasshopper Guard is an inverted leg-lock entry where the bottom player threads their legs around a standing passer's lead leg, secures heel control, and rotates into ashi garami to attack the knee ligaments through lateral rotation.
source.description: Master the heel hook from grasshopper guard with inverted entry mechanics, leg entanglement transitions, finishing details, and essential safety protocols.
source.target_area: Ankle joint, knee ligaments (ACL/MCL/LCL), and lower leg structural integrity
source.overview:
The heel hook from grasshopper guard exploits the unique inverted angles available when playing this unorthodox open guard. The bottom player uses elevated hips and a shoulder-based foundation to thread legs around the opponent's lead leg, securing heel control from an angle that standard guard positions cannot provide. The inversion creates access to lateral heel exposure that conventional ashi garami entries require multiple transitional steps to achieve, compressing the attack chain into a single fluid motion from guard to finish.

What distinguishes this entry from conventional heel hook setups is the deception inherent in the grasshopper configuration. The opponent perceives a guard retention or sweep attempt rather than a direct submission threat, delaying their defensive reactions by critical fractions of a second. The grasshopper position allows the attacker to transition directly from inversion into ashi garami while maintaining constant proximity to the heel, eliminating the usual warning signals that accompany standard leg lock entries.

Strategically, this submission functions best within a broader grasshopper guard attack system. When the opponent defends sweeps by posting or widening their base, they inadvertently expose their lead leg to entanglement. The heel hook threat forces a choice between maintaining sweep defense or protecting the legs, creating an offensive dilemma that elevates success rates across all attack paths from this position.

injury_risks.recovery_time: 6-12 months with surgical reconstruction, extensive rehabilitation
3-6 months for grade 3 tears, potential permanent instability

injury_risks.injury: Meniscus tear (cartilage damage in knee joint)
injury_risks.recovery_time: 4-8 weeks to 6 months depending on severity and treatment

injury_risks.injury: Ankle ligament damage and joint capsule injury
Tibial/fibular fracture from extreme rotational force

safety_considerations.application_speed: EXTREMELY SLOW and progressive - minimum 5-7 seconds from initial pressure to maximum force in training. NEVER apply sudden rotational force.
tap_signals: Verbal tap (primary signal)
Physical hand tap on opponent or mat
Physical foot tap with free leg
Any distress vocalization
Frantic slapping or waving with hands
Leg stiffening or immediate defensive reaction
release_protocol: Immediately stop all rotational pressure upon any tap signal
Release heel grip completely before releasing leg entanglement
Slowly unwrap leg configuration while maintaining awareness of opponent's joint
Allow opponent to extract their leg at their own pace
Check with training partner about their knee and ankle status
Report any joint discomfort to instructor immediately, even if minor
training_restrictions: NEVER apply sudden or explosive rotational force in training
NEVER practice at competition speed with training partners
NEVER continue pressure if partner's leg begins rotating with the submission
Always allow immediate tap access for both hands
Only train with partners who have explicit experience with heel hook defense
Prohibited for practitioners below brown belt in most traditional academies
Never train heel hooks without instructor supervision during initial learning phases
Stop immediately if any popping, clicking, or unusual sensations occur in opponent's leg

variations_and_setups.description: From grasshopper guard, thread the inside leg across the opponent's lead thigh to access the inside heel, transitioning to inside ashi garami for the inside heel hook finish. This variation attacks with inward rotation and is particularly effective when the opponent's lead leg is positioned with the knee facing inward or their stance is narrow.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: When opponent narrows their stance or their lead knee faces inward, exposing the inside heel

variations_and_setups.variation_name: Outside Heel Hook via Wide Hip Switch
variations_and_setups.description: Execute a wider hip switch during the inversion-to-ashi transition, rotating past the standard inside position to access the outside of the heel. The finishing rotation travels outward rather than inward. This requires more space during the transition but bypasses the standard boot defense that blocks inside entries.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: When opponent successfully defends the inside heel hook by straightening their leg or rotating their knee outward

attacker.name: from Grasshopper Guard Attacker
attacker.description: Learn to execute the heel hook from grasshopper guard. Step-by-step inverted entry mechanics, grip techniques, finishing details, and competition strategies.
attacker.overview: Attacking with the heel hook from grasshopper guard requires precise timing of the inversion-to-entanglement transition. The key advantage is that your inverted positioning gives you access to the opponent's heel from angles they rarely train to defend. Your primary challenge is maintaining heel control during the transition from inverted guard to a stable ashi garami finishing position while preventing the opponent from disengaging or stacking. Success depends on treating the entire sequence from inversion to finish as one continuous motion rather than discrete steps, because any pause between phases allows the opponent to initiate defensive reactions.
key_principles: Secure heel control before transitioning from inversion - premature rotation without grip leads to scrambles and lost position
Use hip elevation as the primary mechanism to create the angle needed for heel access rather than reaching with hands alone
Thread legs to the inside of the opponent's base to prevent easy extraction and stepping away from the entanglement
Execute the transition from grasshopper inversion to ashi garami finishing position as one continuous unbroken motion
Apply rotational pressure using whole-body mechanics from the hip bridge and torso twist rather than arm strength alone
Maintain constant knee pinch throughout the finish to prevent the opponent from straightening or extracting the trapped leg
setup_requirements: Established grasshopper guard with stable shoulder base and hips elevated above chest height
At least one hook engaged behind the opponent's lead knee to anchor the position and prevent disengagement
Opponent's weight committed forward or base narrowed sufficiently to allow leg threading between their stance
Clear path to isolate and control the target heel before the opponent recognizes the submission threat
Sufficient core engagement to maintain inversion throughout the entire transition to the finishing position

execution_steps.description: From open guard, invert your torso onto your shoulder blades while elevating your hips above your chest. Engage your core to maintain hip height and position at least one leg hook behind the opponent's lead knee to prevent them from stepping away. Your arms remain free to transition to heel control in the next phase.

Shoot your inside leg between the opponent's legs, threading it across their lead thigh and positioning your foot behind their far knee. This creates the initial leg entanglement that prevents extraction and establishes the lever arm needed for the heel hook finish. Maintain hip elevation throughout this threading motion.

execution_steps.action: Capture the heel with two-on-one grip
execution_steps.description: Reach both hands to secure the opponent's heel, cupping it with your primary hand while your secondary hand reinforces the grip on the foot and ankle. The heel must be captured before any rotation begins, as attempting to rotate without secure grip control results in a lost position and wasted energy. Pull the heel tight to your chest.

Rotate your hips from the inverted grasshopper position into an inside ashi garami configuration, clamping the opponent's trapped leg between your thighs. This transition must flow as one continuous motion that maintains heel control throughout. Your outside leg crosses over their hip to prevent them from posturing away or creating distance.

execution_steps.action: Lock leg triangle and align the knee
execution_steps.description: Close your legs in a figure-four or triangle configuration around the opponent's trapped leg and squeeze your knees together to eliminate all space. Ensure the opponent's knee is aligned with your chest centerline. This alignment is critical because the rotational force must travel directly through the knee ligaments for the submission to function properly.

Bridge your hips upward while simultaneously rotating the heel laterally using your entire body, not just your arms. The rotation should come from your hip bridge and torso twist working together as a unified system. Apply pressure progressively over several seconds, never jerking or snapping. Monitor your partner's reactions continuously throughout.

If the opponent does not tap, maintain steady pressure and micro-adjust your knee pinch and heel grip. If they begin escaping, be prepared to transition to alternative leg attacks such as a straight ankle lock or kneebar rather than forcing a deteriorating heel hook. Never increase application speed to compensate for positional deterioration. Stop immediately upon any tap signal.

common_counters.counter: Boot defense - opponent straightens trapped leg and drives knee forward to prevent entanglement
common_counters.your_response: Clamp your knees tighter before they fully extend and use your free leg as a secondary hook behind their knee to prevent straightening. If they boot early before your triangle is locked, transition to a straight ankle lock on the extended leg instead.

common_counters.counter: Step back and disengage - opponent retreats to break leg contact before heel grip is established
common_counters.your_response: Follow their retreat by re-inverting and rolling toward them to reestablish leg contact. Use the momentum of their retreat to chase into outside ashi garami or single leg X-guard. Do not abandon inversion to chase standing.

common_counters.counter: Stack pass attempt - opponent drives forward heavily to flatten your inversion and neutralize the attack
common_counters.your_response: Use their forward momentum to complete the hip switch faster, pulling them into your ashi garami as they drive in. Alternatively, convert to a Granby roll to recover guard if they stack before you secure the heel.

common_counters.counter: Counter leg entanglement - opponent threads their own legs to enter 50-50 or reverse entanglement
common_counters.your_response: If they enter 50-50, switch to inside heel hook variant from the shared entanglement. Maintain your original heel grip priority and use the mutual entanglement to your advantage since you initiated the attack first.

common_errors.error: Applying rotation before securing proper heel grip and knee alignment
common_errors.consequence: The opponent extracts their leg easily because there is no mechanical lock preventing escape, wasting the entire attack sequence and returning to neutral
common_errors.correction: Complete all three control checkpoints before any rotation: two-on-one heel grip secured, leg triangle locked with knees squeezed, and opponent's knee aligned to your centerline

common_errors.error: Failing to clamp knees together during the transition from inversion to ashi garami
common_errors.consequence: Creates space that allows the opponent to straighten their leg and pull it free, even with a good heel grip
common_errors.correction: Squeeze your knees together as a constant throughout the entire transition. Think of your thighs as a vise that never loosens from the moment you begin the hip switch

common_errors.error: Staying inverted in grasshopper too long without committing to the heel hook entry
common_errors.consequence: Core fatigue accumulates rapidly in the inverted position, degrading your hip elevation and making the transition to ashi garami weak and slow
common_errors.correction: Treat grasshopper as a 3-5 second launch platform. Enter with the heel hook as your immediate objective and commit fully within that window or transition to a sustainable guard

common_errors.error: Gripping the foot or toes instead of cupping the heel bone directly
common_errors.consequence: Foot and toe grips are slippery and provide insufficient mechanical advantage for rotational force, allowing the opponent to extract with moderate effort
common_errors.correction: Cup the calcaneus (heel bone) in the web of your primary hand with fingers wrapped around the Achilles tendon. The heel is the fixed point that transfers rotation to the knee

common_errors.error: Using arm strength alone for rotational force rather than whole-body mechanics
common_errors.consequence: Arms fatigue quickly and generate insufficient torque to finish against a resisting opponent, resulting in a stalled attack that they can eventually escape
common_errors.correction: Generate rotation from your hip bridge and torso twist working together. Your arms maintain the grip while your body creates the rotational force through bridging and turning

common_errors.error: Neglecting to control the opponent's hip alignment during the finish
common_errors.consequence: The opponent rotates their entire body in the direction of your torque, nullifying the rotational differential needed to stress the knee ligaments
common_errors.correction: Use your legs to pin their hip in place by clamping tightly with the figure-four. Your outside leg crossing their hip prevents them from rotating their body to match your torque direction

training_progressions.focus: Building inverted positioning strength and transition fluency
training_progressions.description: Practice grasshopper guard inversions without a partner, focusing on shoulder base stability, hip elevation endurance, and smooth transitions from inverted to ashi garami body position. Develop the core strength and proprioception needed to maintain control throughout the complete attack sequence.

training_progressions.focus: Heel capture and entanglement from grasshopper at low resistance
training_progressions.description: Work the complete entry sequence from grasshopper guard to heel grip at 30% resistance. Partner stands passively while you practice threading legs, capturing the heel, and transitioning to ashi garami. Focus on grip placement accuracy and smooth continuous motion through each phase without pausing.

training_progressions.focus: Rotational application and proprioceptive sensitivity development
training_progressions.description: From pre-established ashi garami position, practice applying and releasing rotational pressure with extreme control. Partner provides feedback on speed and pressure levels. Build the proprioceptive sensitivity to feel the submission approaching the tap threshold without overshooting into dangerous force levels.

training_progressions.focus: Integration into broader attack system with moderate resistance
training_progressions.description: Practice the full grasshopper attack sequence including sweep threats that set up the heel hook entry. Work transitions between sweep attempts, heel hooks, kneebars, and ankle locks at 60-80% resistance. Partner provides specific defensive reactions to build real-time decision making under pressure.

training_progressions.focus: Full resistance application and competition readiness
training_progressions.description: Begin from grasshopper guard with partner defending at full competition intensity. Work to complete the heel hook or transition to secondary attacks based on defensive reactions. Review each round for timing decisions, grip quality, and attack chain effectiveness.

flashcards.question: What anatomical structures does the heel hook from grasshopper guard primarily attack?
flashcards.answer: The heel hook primarily attacks the knee ligaments, specifically the ACL, MCL, and LCL, through rotational force applied via the heel and ankle. The lateral rotation of the heel creates torsional stress on these ligaments because the foot acts as a lever arm against the fixed knee joint. Secondary stress affects the ankle ligaments and meniscus cartilage.

trap: Muscle strain only, safe to ride

flashcards.question: What physical indicators signal that you have reached the breaking point and should expect a tap?
flashcards.answer: The primary indicator is feeling the opponent's foot begin to rotate freely without muscular resistance, meaning their defensive tension has been overcome. You may also feel a slight give in the knee joint alignment or hear vocalization. At this point, stop increasing pressure immediately and wait for the tap, as the joint is at its structural limit and further force causes irreversible damage.

plausible: Their base collapses to the mat
trap: Crank harder until you hear a pop

flashcards.question: What three control elements must be established before applying any rotational pressure?
flashcards.answer: Before any rotation, you must have a secure two-on-one heel grip with the calcaneus cupped in your primary hand, your legs locked in a figure-four or triangle around the trapped leg with knees squeezed together, and the opponent's knee aligned with your chest centerline. Attempting rotation without all three elements risks losing position or applying force at an angle that permits escape.
flashcards.answer_line: Heel grip, leg triangle, knee align

trap: Grip heel then crank immediately

flashcards.question: At what point during the execution sequence does escape become nearly impossible for the defender?
flashcards.answer: Escape becomes extremely difficult once the attacker completes the hip switch into ashi garami with the leg triangle locked and heel secured. Before this point, the defender can straighten their leg, step back, or rotate their body to clear the entanglement. After the triangle is locked with proper knee alignment, the defender's options narrow to matching rotation or tapping immediately.

plausible: Once the heel alone is gripped
As the hips begin to switch
trap: Never tap, twist out at any stage

flashcards.question: Your heel grip starts slipping during the finish - what adjustment should you make?
flashcards.answer: Immediately stop rotational pressure and re-secure your grip by pulling the heel deeper into your chest or armpit. Use your secondary hand to reinforce by controlling the foot or ankle. Avoid the temptation to grip harder with fingers alone, which fatigues quickly. If the grip cannot be re-established, transition to an ankle lock or release and reset the attack rather than forcing with degraded control.

trap: Force rotation on a slipping grip

flashcards.question: How does establishing the heel grip from grasshopper differ from gripping from standard ashi garami?
flashcards.answer: From grasshopper, the grip is initially established while inverted, meaning your hands approach the heel from an upward angle rather than the standard side angle. During the transition to ashi garami, the grip must be maintained through the hip rotation, requiring elbows tight to your body throughout the movement. The finishing grip position is identical, but the path to reach it demands greater grip awareness during the inversion-to-ashi transition phase.

plausible: Same side angle as standard ashi
trap: Let elbows flare during switch

flashcards.question: Why release all rotational pressure before unwrapping the leg entanglement after a tap?
flashcards.answer: Residual rotational force stored in the twisted position can cause additional ligament damage if released suddenly when the leg configuration changes. The knee joint may be at its structural limit at the moment of tap, and any abrupt change in entanglement geometry while torque remains loaded can tear ligaments even after the tap signal. Always release heel rotation fully first, then slowly unwrap the legs at the opponent's pace.

plausible: Lets the ref confirm the tap
trap: Unwrap the legs all at once

flashcards.question: How should you set up the heel hook in competition to maximize the element of surprise?
flashcards.answer: Chain the heel hook with sweep attempts from grasshopper guard. Begin by threatening an X-guard elevation sweep, which forces the opponent to post and widen their base defensively. This base adjustment exposes their lead leg for the leg thread entry. The opponent perceives guard retention or sweep mechanics rather than a submission threat, buying the seconds needed to secure the initial entanglement before they activate leg lock defense.

plausible: Set up slowly from static guard
trap: Dive for the leg with no control

flashcards.question: Your opponent rotates their body with your heel hook torque—how do you respond?
flashcards.answer: If the opponent rotates with your torque, they are nullifying the rotational differential needed for the submission. Follow their rotation by adjusting your own body angle to maintain the relative twist between their knee and foot. If they continue rotating successfully, transition to a kneebar or switch to the opposite leg rather than forcing additional torque against a rotating opponent, which wastes energy without progress.
flashcards.answer_line: Follow their spin, keep the twist

trap: Release to scramble for the back

flashcards.question: What is the most common reason the heel hook from grasshopper guard fails at the finishing stage?
flashcards.answer: The most common failure is insufficient knee pinch during the finish, which allows the opponent to straighten their leg and extract it from the entanglement. Many practitioners focus entirely on heel grip and rotational force while neglecting the leg clamp that prevents extraction. Without tight knees squeezing the trapped leg between your thighs, even a perfect heel grip fails as the opponent simply extends their leg out of the submission.

trap: Releasing knees to reset angle

defender.name: from Grasshopper Guard Defender
defender.description: Defend the heel hook from grasshopper guard. Recognition cues, escape techniques, boot defense mechanics, and critical safety protocols for knee protection.
defender.overview: Defending the heel hook from grasshopper guard demands early recognition and immediate response. The inverted entry disguises the submission threat as a guard retention or sweep attempt, making early detection critical for survival. Your primary defensive priorities are preventing the initial leg entanglement, maintaining your base against the sweep threats that precede the heel hook, and knowing when to abandon technical defense and tap to protect your knee. The rotational force on the knee ligaments develops rapidly once the ashi garami position is secured, making late-stage escapes extremely dangerous and reinforcing the importance of defending early or tapping decisively.
key_principles: Recognize the heel hook setup before the heel grip is established - prevention is far more effective than late escape
Keep your lead leg straight and your base wide to prevent leg threading from the inverted position
Never attempt explosive extraction once the attacker has secured heel grip and locked their leg triangle
Match the direction of rotation rather than fighting against it when caught in the finishing position
Tap early and decisively - knee ligament damage occurs before pain signals arrive and is often career-altering
Maintain awareness of your knee alignment relative to the attacker's body to gauge escape viability
recognition_cues: Opponent inverts onto their shoulders and elevates hips while maintaining leg contact with your lead leg
Feel a hook threading behind your lead knee from an unusual upward angle as they begin the entanglement
Opponent's hands shift from guard grips to reaching toward your heel, foot, or ankle area
Visible hip rotation as the opponent begins transitioning from inverted position toward ashi garami configuration
Sudden clamping pressure around your lead thigh as their legs close into a triangle or figure-four

defensive_options.action: Boot defense - straighten the trapped leg and drive your knee forward before the entanglement locks
defensive_options.when_to_use: Early stage when you feel the initial leg thread but before the attacker secures heel grip
defensive_options.if_successful: Clears the leg from the entanglement and forces attacker to reset from grasshopper guard
defensive_options.risk: If attempted too late after the triangle is locked, the straightening motion can worsen knee exposure

defensive_options.action: Rotation matching - turn your body in the same direction as the attacker's torque to neutralize rotational differential
defensive_options.when_to_use: Mid to late stage when the attacker has grip but before full rotation is applied
defensive_options.if_successful: Nullifies the submission pressure and may create opening to extract the leg as the attacker readjusts
defensive_options.risk: Requires precise directional awareness and may lead to positional scramble

defensive_options.action: Drive forward to closed guard - push your hips forward and close your legs around the opponent's torso
defensive_options.when_to_use: When the opponent is still partially inverted and has not completed the hip switch to ashi garami
defensive_options.if_successful: Neutralizes the inverted attack angles entirely and forces the opponent to abandon the heel hook to address guard position
defensive_options.risk: Requires committing your weight forward which can complete a sweep if the opponent transitions

escape_paths: Straighten the trapped leg and step backward to extract from the entanglement before heel grip is secured
Rotate your entire body in the direction of applied torque to neutralize the rotational differential on the knee
Drive forward to flatten the opponent's inversion and close guard around their torso to eliminate attack angles

favorable_outcomes.how: Drive your hips forward to flatten the opponent's inversion, close your legs around their torso, and establish closed guard top position which completely neutralizes the inverted heel hook threat
Successfully boot the entanglement early by straightening your leg and stepping back, forcing the attacker to reset in grasshopper guard without submission progress

common_errors.error: Attempting to explosively rip the leg free once the attacker has secured heel grip and locked the triangle
common_errors.consequence: Explosive extraction dramatically accelerates ligament damage because the rotational force on the knee increases exponentially with speed, potentially causing ACL rupture
common_errors.correction: If the heel grip and triangle are locked, focus on controlled rotation matching to neutralize torque. If escape is not viable, tap immediately rather than risking permanent knee damage

common_errors.error: Failing to recognize the submission threat due to the inverted entry disguising it as a sweep attempt
common_errors.consequence: Delays defensive reaction until the attacker has already secured heel grip and transitioned to ashi garami, eliminating early-stage prevention options
common_errors.correction: Train specific recognition of grasshopper-to-heel-hook patterns. When you see an opponent invert with leg hooks near your knee, immediately assume a leg lock threat and begin preventive defense

common_errors.error: Keeping a narrow stance when facing grasshopper guard, making leg threading easy
common_errors.consequence: A narrow base allows the inverted opponent to thread their legs between yours with minimal resistance, accelerating the entanglement sequence
common_errors.correction: Maintain a wide base when facing grasshopper guard and keep your lead leg active, ready to straighten and step back at the first sign of leg threading

common_errors.error: Waiting to feel pain before tapping to the heel hook
common_errors.consequence: Knee ligament damage frequently occurs before pain signals reach the brain, meaning significant structural damage has already happened by the time you feel discomfort
common_errors.correction: Tap based on positional awareness rather than pain. If you feel rotational pressure on your knee that you cannot counter technically, tap immediately regardless of competitive context

flashcards.question: How do you recognize that a heel hook attempt is developing from grasshopper guard?
flashcards.answer: Watch for the opponent's hands shifting from guard grips to reaching toward your heel or ankle while their legs thread around your lead leg. The key transition signal is their hip switch from inverted position toward ashi garami, visible as a rotation in their lower body. The earlier you detect this shift in hand and hip movement, the more defensive options remain available to you.
flashcards.answer_line: Hands to heel, hip switch begins

trap: Wait for heel grip to react

flashcards.question: What is the safest response when you feel rotational pressure on your knee that you cannot counter?
flashcards.answer: Tap immediately and clearly using verbal and physical signals simultaneously. Say tap loudly while slapping your hand on the opponent or the mat repeatedly. Do not wait to feel pain, as knee ligament damage often occurs before pain signals reach your brain. If you feel any rotational pressure on your knee that you cannot neutralize through rotation matching or extraction, tap immediately regardless of competitive context.

plausible: Kick the free leg to break grips
Sit up and pry the ankle loose
trap: Wait until you feel real pain

flashcards.question: What is your primary defensive action when you feel the initial leg thread from grasshopper guard?
flashcards.answer: Immediately straighten your threatened leg and step it backward, removing it from the opponent's entanglement range. This boot defense must happen before they secure heel grip, because once the heel is captured and the triangle locked, your escape options diminish rapidly. Combine the leg straightening with a back step to create distance from their inverted position.

trap: Yank leg out explosively

flashcards.question: Why is it dangerous to try to explode out of a partially locked heel hook?
flashcards.answer: Explosive movement against a secured heel hook dramatically accelerates ligament damage. The rotational force on the knee increases exponentially with the speed of extraction, and a sudden pull can tear the ACL faster than you can register pain or faster than the attacker can release. Controlled methodical escape by matching rotation and slowly extracting is far safer than any explosive reaction.

trap: Rip free before the pain hits

flashcards.question: What position should you work toward when caught in the early stages of this heel hook?
flashcards.answer: Work to establish closed guard by driving your hips forward and closing your legs around the opponent's torso, which negates their inversion advantage and eliminates the angles needed for leg entanglement attacks. This forces them to abandon the heel hook entirely to address the guard position change. Alternatively, stand up with wide base while clearing their hooks to eliminate the inversion-based attack.

plausible: Invert with them to match angles
trap: Turn away and roll to escape

training_progressions.focus: Early detection of heel hook setup cues from grasshopper guard
training_progressions.description: Partner establishes grasshopper guard and slowly demonstrates each stage of the heel hook entry sequence. Builds pattern recognition for the specific visual and tactile cues that distinguish heel hook setups from sweep attempts.

training_progressions.description: Partner attempts heel hook entry from grasshopper at increasing resistance levels starting at 30%. Defender focuses exclusively on straightening the threatened leg and stepping back before heel grip is secured. Progressively increase to 70% resistance over multiple sessions while maintaining clean defensive technique.

training_progressions.focus: Methodical escape from partially secured positions without explosive movement
training_progressions.description: Partner secures various stages of the heel hook and holds position. Defender practices rotation matching, controlled leg extraction, and guard recovery using slow deliberate movement only. Emphasis on safety-first escapes that prioritize joint protection over competitive positioning.

training_progressions.focus: Integrating all defensive skills against realistic heel hook attempts
training_progressions.description: Begin from grasshopper guard position with partner attempting heel hooks at 80% intensity. Defender applies recognition, prevention, boot defense, and escape skills in realistic context. Review each exchange for defensive timing, tap decision quality, and identification of the latest viable escape point.

source.name: Anaconda Choke from Dead Orchard
source.description: Anaconda Choke from Dead Orchard needs a separate front headlock. Its arm-and-neck enclosure differs from the bottom player's high both-arm leg triangle.
source.summary: The Anaconda Choke is an arm-triangle choke from a front headlock, using an arm threaded under the neck and out by the armpit to enclose the head and one arm.
source.target_area: Sides of the neck between the attacking arm and trapped shoulder
source.overview:
The attacker controls the head and one arm from in front of the opponent, with room to establish the arm enclosure and a safe rolling angle. Dead Orchard is a bottom-player high leg triangle containing both arms. Its leg enclosure does not supply an Anaconda grip; a separate front-headlock exchange must occur first.

Contain the opponent's head and one arm while keeping a balanced base. Pass the choking arm beneath the neck and toward the far armpit, enclosing one shoulder. Join to the supporting arm without pulling the neck into a twist. Use the taught shoulder-led angle only when both partners can roll safely; do not dive onto the neck.

Introduce the arm loop without pressure and rehearse any roll cooperatively. Never drive onto the cervical spine or continue squeezing after a tap.

Instructional sources: [Stephan Kesting and Denis Kang — the Anaconda choke](https://www.grapplearts.com/the-anaconda-choke/); [Nathan Orchard — Dead Orchard, part 1](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XoiB1D2WJwE).

injury_risks.injury: Neck injury during a forced roll or head twist
injury_risks.recovery_time: Variable; stop training and seek appropriate clinical assessment after an injury or concerning symptoms.

injury_risks.injury: Loss of consciousness or serious harm from a sustained choke
injury_risks.recovery_time: Variable; stop training and seek appropriate clinical assessment after an injury or concerning symptoms.

safety_considerations.application_speed: Introduce the arm loop without pressure and rehearse any roll cooperatively. Never drive onto the cervical spine or continue squeezing after a tap. No fixed number of seconds makes a locked submission safe.
tap_signals: Repeated hand taps anywhere the partner can feel them
A clear verbal tap or stop, including when the hands are trapped
Foot taps or any agreed stop signal; release immediately if normal responsiveness changes
release_protocol: Open the finishing grip immediately at the first signal; do not wait for repeated confirmation
Remove the leg, arm or body restraint without forcing the captured joint or neck through another movement
Check the partner can respond normally and allow a safe reset; end practice and obtain help if there is an injury or concerning symptom
training_restrictions: Start with supervised, cooperative control-and-release drilling rather than a loaded finish
Check the event's current rules for the specific age, experience and clothing division before live use
Introduce the arm loop without pressure and rehearse any roll cooperatively. Never drive onto the cervical spine or continue squeezing after a tap.

source.name: Calf Slicer from Carni
source.summary: The Calf Slicer folds a controlled leg around a shin or forearm placed behind the knee, creating calf compression and potentially dangerous loading of the knee joint.
source.description: Calf Slicer from Carni requires a separate leg capture. Carni controls a shoulder; calf compression needs a shin or forearm behind a folded, controlled knee.
source.overview:
The attacker controls a bent opposing leg with a shin or forearm in the knee fold and a connection that limits the heel moving away. Carni controls an upper-body shoulder. A slicer requires a separate lower-body capture; the fold behind the opponent's knee cannot be inferred from a rubber-guard shoulder clamp.

Control the opposing thigh and lower leg in a genuine leg-entanglement position. Position the shin or forearm behind the knee without forcing the joint sideways. Keep the attacking leg stable so resistance does not twist your own knee. Identify how the lower leg folds toward the thigh without pulling it to end range.

A calf slicer can injure the knee as well as hurt the calf. Use control-only drilling, protect both partners' knees and respect division restrictions.

source.overview:
The initial Dead Orchard Control configuration must be identified before considering Darce Control. The defining feature is both shoulders and arms enclosed by the legs. An anaconda instead uses an arm loop around the neck and one arm from a front headlock; the two controls require different body configurations. The reviewed instruction does not establish a direct Dead Orchard Control-to-Darce Control connection. Release the original lock safely and establish the destination's own prerequisites; do not treat these checkpoints as a demonstrated continuous entry.

The legs form a high figure-four around the shoulder line, with both opposing arms inside. Both arms may be trapped, so agree on verbal and foot taps. Never stack the neck, wrench a knee into the leg triangle, or test a captured elbow by pulling hard. Open the original connection before either partner turns, rises or changes the captured limb.

Move through available space with a stable base. Stop and release any trapped neck, shoulder or knee before changing direction; do not force a roll or stack to preserve the route.

source.summary: The leg-weave pass uses an arm threaded between the legs to bring the knees together, then clears the remaining foot or half-guard hook before settling into side control.

The top passer begins in Leg Weave, facing a knee shield or linked leg frame. The weaving limb is the arm. Securing that control is the entry checkpoint; a pass is complete only after the hips and remaining leg hooks are cleared.

The passer's arm connecting your legs is the relevant control, not a leg threaded across your hip. Maintain a useful knee angle and upper-body frame before the passer folds the legs together. Move the hips and pummel the knee back between the bodies while the weave is still loose.

Prevent the passer from flattening your shoulders while controlling the legs. An underhook can help you face the passer and rebuild half guard when the shoulder line is not already pinned. Do not wrench a knee out of a fixed weave; create room with the hips and frames first.

source.name: Turtle to Aoki Lock
source.description: Enter the Aoki Lock from Turtle Top in no-gi BJJ. Isolate the arm, thread your leg over the shoulder, and entangle to secure this leg-trapped shoulder lock control.
source.summary: Turtle to Aoki Lock is a no-gi entry in which the top player attacking a turtled opponent isolates the near arm, threads a leg over the shoulder, and entangles the limb to secure the leg-trapped shoulder lock control.
source.overview:
Turtle to Aoki Lock is the primary leg-entanglement entry into the Aoki Lock shoulder-lock control, executed by the top player who is breaking down or attacking a turtled opponent. From a strong front-headlock or side-riding position over the turtle, the attacker isolates the opponent's near arm, drives a knee in front of the far shoulder, and threads a leg over the trapped arm to create the signature leg-over-shoulder entanglement that defines the Aoki Lock. Named after Shinya Aoki, who popularized leg-trapped shoulder locks in MMA, this entry converts the relatively neutral turtle exchange into a high-control submission state.

The entry exploits the fact that a turtling opponent must keep their elbows tight to protect their neck and back, but in doing so they leave the shoulder girdle accessible to a vertical leg trap. By stuffing the head, peeling the near arm away from the body, and stepping the leg over, the attacker isolates the shoulder complex before the opponent can return to a tight defensive shell. Timing is critical: the leg must come over while the arm is extended and before the opponent can either re-tuck the elbow or explode out the back door to attack the legs.

Because the turtle is a scramble-heavy position, this entry carries genuine risk. A premature or loose leg trap invites the opponent to roll through, attack the entangling leg, or scramble to the attacker's back. Done correctly, however, it lands the attacker in dominant Aoki Lock top control with immediate finishing, back-take, truck, and crucifix threats, making it one of the highest-value sequences available against a defensive turtle in modern no-gi grappling.
conditions: Attacker has established top control over a turtled opponent, ideally with a front headlock or side-ride
Opponent's near arm can be peeled away from their body and extended
Attacker has a free leg available to thread over the opponent's shoulder
Opponent has not yet exploded back to standing or initiated a scramble to the legs

attacker.name: Turtle to Aoki Lock Attacker
attacker.description: How to enter the Aoki Lock from Turtle Top in no-gi. Arm isolation, leg-over-shoulder entanglement, and finishing setup with counters and common errors.
attacker.overview:
As the attacker, your goal is to convert top control over a turtled opponent into the leg-entangled Aoki Lock shoulder lock. The sequence hinges on isolating the near arm, breaking it away from the opponent's tight defensive shell, and threading your leg over their shoulder to trap the arm vertically against your hip and thigh. This is a no-gi specialty entry that rewards aggressive arm-hunting and precise timing over strength.

The controlling concept is that a turtling opponent protects their neck and back by keeping elbows pinned, which paradoxically presents the shoulder joint as the weak link. Once you peel the elbow up and away, the shoulder loses its protective alignment and your leg can cross over to trap it. From there, you sit your hips back and rotate, loading omoplata-style pressure onto the isolated shoulder while your legs form the entanglement that gives the position its control.

Speed and commitment matter because the turtle is inherently scramble-prone. Hesitating after you peel the arm lets the opponent re-tuck the elbow or spin to your back. The most reliable entries come from a strong front headlock or side-ride where you have already compromised the opponent's posture and isolated the head and one arm before stepping the leg over.
key_principles: Isolate and extend the opponent's near arm before attempting to step your leg over - a tucked elbow blocks the entry
Stuff the head and control posture first so the opponent cannot stand up or spin out during the entry
Thread your leg over the shoulder, not the bicep, to trap the full shoulder complex and create rotational leverage
Sit your hips back and rotate as the leg crosses to load omoplata-style pressure and tighten the entanglement
Keep your legs actively squeezing the trapped arm so the opponent cannot extract before you settle
Commit decisively once the arm is peeled - hesitation invites the back-door scramble to your back
Control the far hip or far side with your hands to prevent the opponent from rolling through the entanglement
setup_requirements: Top control established over a turtled opponent, ideally with a front headlock or tight side-ride
The opponent's near arm peeled away from their torso and extended enough to thread a leg over
Your hips positioned close to the opponent's shoulder so your thigh can cross the shoulder line
A free leg available and unweighted, ready to step over the trapped arm
Head and posture control on the opponent so they cannot drive forward to stand or roll backward

execution_steps.action: Break down the turtle and establish a front headlock
execution_steps.description: From top position over the turtled opponent, drive your weight forward and snag a front headlock or tight chin-strap, flattening their posture so their head is low and their hips cannot rise. This removes their ability to stand up and forces them to commit to defending in the turtle shell, where their arms become accessible.

execution_steps.action: Isolate and peel the near arm
execution_steps.description: Reach across and dig your hand under the opponent's near elbow, then peel the arm up and away from their ribs. You must break it free of the tight defensive tuck so the shoulder loses its protective alignment. Pin the wrist or upper arm against your body so the limb stays extended and cannot be re-tucked once you commit to the leg.

execution_steps.action: Drive your knee in front of the shoulder
execution_steps.description: Step your near-side knee forward so it lands in front of the opponent's isolated shoulder, creating a wedge between their arm and their body. This knee wedge prevents the arm from returning and prepares the lane for your shin and thigh to cross over the shoulder line on the next step.

execution_steps.action: Thread the leg over the shoulder
execution_steps.description: With the arm extended and the knee wedged, swing your free leg over the top of the opponent's shoulder so your thigh lands across the back of their shoulder and your shin controls the upper arm. This is the defining moment of the Aoki Lock entry - the leg-over-shoulder trap isolates the entire shoulder complex rather than just the bicep.

execution_steps.action: Lock the entanglement and sit to your hip
execution_steps.description: Cross or triangle your legs around the trapped arm to lock the entanglement, then sit your hips back toward the mat on the trapped-arm side. Sitting back loads rotational, omoplata-style pressure onto the shoulder and removes the opponent's ability to follow you and relieve the tension. Keep your legs squeezing throughout so the arm cannot slide out.

execution_steps.action: Settle into Aoki Lock control and manage the far side
execution_steps.description: Post your free leg for base and reach to control the opponent's far hip or far-side limb with your hands, killing their ability to roll through the entanglement. Settle your weight to consolidate the Aoki Lock top control, from which you can now threaten the finish, the back take, the truck, or the crucifix.

common_counters.counter: Opponent re-tucks the elbow tight to their ribs before you can thread the leg
common_counters.your_response: Maintain your peel and use your knee wedge to keep the lane open; if the elbow is fully recovered, abandon the leg-over and switch to a front-headlock attack or back take rather than forcing a closed entry.

common_counters.counter: Opponent explodes backward and spins to attack your back as you commit the leg
common_counters.your_response: Recognize the spin early and either follow to maintain top control over the turtle, or if they win the angle, fight hands immediately to deny the seatbelt and prevent them from securing your back.

common_counters.counter: Opponent grips your entangling leg and tries to strip it off the shoulder
common_counters.your_response: Sit deeper to your hip and apply the rotational shoulder pressure so they must release the grip to defend the joint; tighten the leg triangle so the limb cannot be peeled away.

common_counters.counter: Opponent drives forward to stand and run out the front door
common_counters.your_response: Your prior head and posture control should already deny this; if they begin to rise, re-flatten the head with the front headlock and reset the arm isolation before re-attempting the leg-over.

common_errors.error: Stepping the leg over before the arm is peeled and extended
common_errors.consequence: The trapped arm stays tucked and the entanglement isolates only the bicep, giving the opponent an easy arm extraction and escape back to turtle.
common_errors.correction: Always peel and extend the near arm fully and wedge your knee in front of the shoulder before threading the leg, so the leg traps the whole shoulder complex.

common_errors.error: Neglecting head and posture control during the entry
common_errors.consequence: The opponent stands up or drives forward out the front door, completely escaping the entry and resetting to a neutral scramble.
common_errors.correction: Secure a front headlock or chin-strap and flatten the opponent's posture first, keeping their head low throughout the arm isolation and leg-over steps.

common_errors.error: Hesitating after peeling the arm instead of committing to the leg-over
common_errors.consequence: The pause gives the opponent time to re-tuck the elbow or spin to your back, turning a dominant entry into a scramble you may lose.
common_errors.correction: Treat the peel and the leg-over as one continuous, committed motion - once the arm is free, the leg must come over immediately.

common_errors.error: Failing to control the far hip after the entanglement is set
common_errors.consequence: The opponent rolls through the trapped shoulder and either escapes or reverses, since nothing prevents them turning into the entanglement.
common_errors.correction: As you settle, reach to control the far hip or far-side limb with your hands and post your free leg to kill the roll-through escape.

common_errors.error: Applying rotational shoulder pressure explosively as soon as you settle
common_errors.consequence: A sudden crank risks a serious shoulder injury to your partner before they can recognize and tap, which is both dangerous and unsporting.
common_errors.correction: Settle the control first, then apply shoulder pressure gradually over several seconds while watching for tap signals, releasing immediately on any tap.

common_errors.error: Letting the leg triangle loosen while you reach to control the far side
common_errors.consequence: The opponent extracts the trapped arm through the gap and escapes to turtle or to your back during the transition.
common_errors.correction: Keep your legs actively squeezing the trapped arm the entire time; only reach with one hand at a time so leg tension is never sacrificed for grip.

Practice reading and beating each defense, and recognizing when to abandon the entry for a back take or front headlock attack instead. 3-minute rounds, multiple per session.

training_progressions.focus: Hitting the entry in live scrambles from the turtle

Work to set up the front headlock, isolate the arm, and hit the Aoki Lock entry against a fully resisting, scrambling opponent. Develop timing, transition awareness, and safe finishing under pressure.

flashcards.question: Why must you peel and extend the opponent's near arm before threading your leg over the shoulder?
flashcards.answer: A turtling opponent keeps their elbows tucked tight to protect the neck and back, which also keeps the shoulder in a protected alignment. If you step the leg over before peeling the arm, you trap only the bicep and the opponent can easily extract. Peeling and extending the arm first breaks the protective alignment so the leg-over isolates the entire shoulder complex, which is what gives the Aoki Lock its control and finishing leverage.

trap: Wait for arm to relax

flashcards.question: What role does the front headlock or head control play in the Turtle to Aoki Lock entry?
flashcards.answer: Head and posture control via a front headlock flattens the opponent and removes their primary turtle escapes: standing up and driving forward out the front door. With the head pinned low, the opponent is forced to defend in the shell where their arm is accessible, and they cannot generate the upward drive needed to escape while you peel the arm and step the leg over. Without this control, the opponent simply stands and runs out of the entry.

trap: Let go to free your hands

flashcards.question: What is the biggest risk if you hesitate after peeling the arm, and how do you avoid it?
flashcards.answer: Hesitation gives the opponent time to either re-tuck their elbow tight to the ribs, restoring their defensive shell, or explode backward and spin to attack your back, turning a dominant entry into a losing scramble. You avoid this by treating the arm peel and the leg-over as a single continuous, committed motion - the moment the arm is free and extended, the leg comes over immediately and the entanglement locks before the opponent can react.
flashcards.answer_line: Commit peel and leg-over as one

trap: Wait for opponent to settle

flashcards.question: After locking the entanglement, why is controlling the far hip important?
flashcards.answer: Once your legs trap the shoulder, the opponent's primary escape is to roll through the entanglement by turning into it. Reaching to control the far hip or far-side limb, combined with posting your free leg, kills that roll-through by removing the opponent's ability to turn and reverse. Without far-side control, the opponent can spin out of the trapped shoulder and escape to turtle or even to your back during the transition.

trap: Release grips to reset

flashcards.question: How should you apply the shoulder pressure safely once you have settled into Aoki Lock control?
flashcards.answer: Settle and consolidate the control first, then apply the rotational, omoplata-style shoulder pressure gradually over several seconds using a controlled hip rotation rather than an explosive crank. Watch your partner constantly for verbal or physical tap signals and release immediately on any tap. The shoulder joint is fragile and a sudden application can cause rotator cuff tears, labrum damage, or dislocation before the partner can react, so progressive pressure is mandatory.
flashcards.answer_line: Add pressure slowly, watch for taps

plausible: Push straight down on the joint
trap: Crank explosively

attacker.safety_considerations: The Aoki Lock is a shoulder lock and carries genuine injury risk - rotator cuff tears, labrum damage, and shoulder dislocation are all possible if pressure is applied too fast or held past the tap. Apply the rotational shoulder pressure gradually over several seconds and release instantly on any verbal or physical tap. Because this entry happens in a scramble-heavy turtle exchange, also protect both players' necks during the front headlock phase by never cranking the neck for control, and ensure adequate mat space since the leg-over and roll-through reactions cover ground.

defender.name: Turtle to Aoki Lock Defender
defender.description: Defend the Aoki Lock entry from Turtle Bottom in no-gi. Recognize the arm peel and leg-over, keep your elbow tucked, and escape before the shoulder lock entanglement locks.
defender.overview:
As the defender, you are in the turtle being attacked by a top player who is hunting your near arm to enter the Aoki Lock shoulder lock. Your entire defense rests on protecting the shoulder by keeping your elbows tucked tight to your body and denying the attacker the extended arm they need to thread their leg over. Once the leg crosses your shoulder and the entanglement locks, you are in a dangerous, hard-to-escape control, so the battle must be won during the entry, not after.

The key recognition is feeling the attacker dig under your near elbow and try to peel your arm away from your ribs. The moment you sense this, you must fight to keep the elbow glued to your side and your shoulder rolled under, because an exposed, extended arm is exactly what the entry requires. If they wedge a knee in front of your shoulder, the leg-over is imminent and you must act immediately by either re-tucking, exploding out, or spinning to deny the entanglement.

Because the turtle is a scramble position, your best escapes are dynamic: spinning to face the attacker, exploding backward to attack their back, or standing up before they flatten your head. The worst outcome is staying static while they isolate the arm. Defended early and aggressively, this entry is low-percentage; defended late, after the leg is over, you may be forced to tap to protect the shoulder.
key_principles: Keep your elbows tucked tight to your ribs - an extended arm is the prerequisite the attacker needs
Roll your near shoulder under and protect the joint the instant you feel the arm being peeled
Recognize the knee-wedge in front of your shoulder as the final warning before the leg comes over
Stay dynamic - spin, stand, or explode rather than defending statically inside the shell
Fight the head and posture control early so you retain the option to stand up and out
Tap early if the leg-over locks and shoulder pressure builds - the joint is not worth an injury
recognition_cues: You feel the top player dig a hand under your near elbow and begin peeling the arm away from your ribs
The attacker drives a knee forward so it wedges in front of your shoulder, blocking your arm from re-tucking
You sense the attacker's hips lowering and a leg beginning to swing over the top of your shoulder line

favorable_outcomes.how: Defend the entry by keeping your elbow tucked and your shoulder protected so the attacker fails to peel the arm, forcing them to abandon the leg-over and reset. Stay heavy and mobile in the turtle so you retain the option to stand or spin.

Time the attacker's forward commitment to the leg-over and explode backward, spinning behind them to take the back. The same forward weight that powers their entry creates the lane for your spin if you act decisively.

common_errors.consequence: The exposed, extendable arm is exactly what the attacker needs, and they can peel it and thread the leg over to enter the Aoki Lock.
common_errors.correction: Keep both elbows pinned tight to your sides at all times in the turtle, treating the arm as the single most important thing to protect.

common_errors.error: Defending statically inside the shell instead of moving
common_errors.consequence: A static turtle gives the attacker unlimited time to isolate the arm, wedge the knee, and complete the leg-over entry.
common_errors.correction: Stay dynamic - constantly threaten to stand, spin, or explode backward so the attacker cannot settle into the methodical arm isolation.

common_errors.error: Waiting too long to tap once the leg is over and the shoulder is loaded
common_errors.consequence: Once the entanglement is locked and rotational pressure builds, defending past the safe range risks rotator cuff tears, labrum damage, or dislocation.
common_errors.correction: If the leg-over locks and you cannot immediately spin or extract, tap early to protect the shoulder rather than enduring dangerous joint pressure.

flashcards.question: Why is a tucked elbow the key defense against the Aoki Lock entry from turtle?
flashcards.answer: The entry requires the attacker to peel your near arm away from your ribs and extend it so they can thread a leg over the shoulder and trap the whole shoulder complex. If your elbow stays glued to your side and your shoulder is rolled under, there is no extended arm to trap, the knee-wedge has nothing to exploit, and the leg-over cannot isolate the shoulder. Protecting the tucked elbow denies the prerequisite for the entire technique.

trap: Extend arm to create space

flashcards.question: What is the final warning sign that the leg-over is imminent, and how should you respond?
flashcards.answer: The final warning is feeling the attacker wedge a knee in front of your shoulder, which blocks your arm from re-tucking and clears the lane for the leg to come over. When you feel that knee wedge, you must act immediately - either explode backward to spin to their back using their forward commitment, or stand up and drive out the front door before the leg crosses. Waiting passively at this point almost guarantees the entanglement locks.

trap: Stay still and brace

flashcards.question: When should you stop defending and tap during this sequence?
flashcards.answer: You should tap early once the leg-over has locked the entanglement and you feel rotational pressure building on the shoulder without an immediate spin or extraction available. The Aoki Lock is a true shoulder lock that can cause rotator cuff tears, labrum damage, or dislocation, and these injuries occur quickly once pressure is applied. If you cannot escape the moment the lock is set, protecting the joint by tapping is the correct decision rather than risking a serious shoulder injury.
flashcards.answer_line: Tap once the lock is set

plausible: Wait until you feel a pop
trap: Fight through the pressure

variants_and_adaptations.description: Establish a tight front headlock first to flatten the opponent's posture, then peel the now-exposed near arm and step the leg over the shoulder. source.position_integration: The Turtle to Aoki Lock entry is the principal feeder transition that makes the Aoki Lock control reachable from the standard top-turtle attacking framework. It slots directly into the front-headlock and side-ride system that strong no-gi top players already use against the turtle, offering a shoulder-lock branch alongside the more familiar back-take and front-headlock-choke options. Once the entry succeeds, it connects forward into the full Aoki Lock attack tree - the direct shoulder-lock finish, the back take when the opponent defends the joint, the truck entry, and the crucifix when the far arm exposes - making this transition the gateway that links the turtle exchange to an entire advanced control-and-finishing system in modern no-gi grappling.

source.summary: Kiss of the Dragon is a reverse De La Riva inversion that takes the bottom player underneath the opponent's near leg to reach the backside and pursue rear control.
source.description: Kiss of the Dragon is a reverse De La Riva inversion that takes the bottom player underneath the opponent's near leg to reach the backside and pursue rear control.
source.overview:
The bottom player has a reverse De La Riva hook against a standing or crouching passer, with space for shoulder-supported inversion. It begins from guard below the opponent, not from a top turtle ride. Reaching behind the legs is a checkpoint; complete back control still requires torso attachment and leg control.

Use the reverse hook and lower-leg connection while facing the standing passer. Load weight onto the far leg or available post to create space beside the near leg. Turn onto the shoulder and upper back, keeping weight off the neck.

Move through available space with a stable base. Stop and release any trapped neck, shoulder or knee before changing direction; do not force a roll or stack to preserve the route.

Instructional sources: [Giancarlo Bodoni — reverse De La Riva inversion](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vkT6Mpn5uLY); [Rob Biernacki and Stephan Kesting — no-gi De La Riva](https://www.grapplearts.com/no-gi-de-la-riva/).

source.name: Technical Standup from Inversion
source.description: Learn Technical Standup from Inversion in BJJ. Step-by-step execution from Inverted Guard to standing with complete attacker and defender analysis.
source.summary: Technical Standup from Inversion is a guard-exit technique where a inverted-guard player channels their inverted momentum into a hip-under rotation and a posted hand to rise to a standing open guard before distance or fatigue turns the inversion into a liability.
source.overview:
The Technical Standup from Inversion is a critical transitional skill that allows a inverted guard player to safely exit the inverted position and return to a standing open guard engagement. When the opponent disengages or creates too much distance for effective leg attacks from inverted guard, remaining inverted becomes a liability rather than an asset. This technique bridges the gap between the high-energy inverted posture and a sustainable standing guard where the practitioner can reset their offensive options.

The movement requires coordinating a hip-over-shoulder rotation with precise posting mechanics to avoid exposing the back or collapsing into a vulnerable position during the transition. Unlike a standard technical standup from seated guard, the inverted starting point adds complexity because the practitioner must first rotate their hips underneath them before establishing the posting base. The inversion creates momentum that, when properly channeled, actually accelerates the standup sequence rather than hindering it.

Strategically, this technique serves as the essential exit valve for inverted guard. Without a reliable standup pathway, the inverted player becomes trapped in a position that drains energy rapidly. Knowing when to abandon the inversion and come up to feet is often what separates effective inverted guard players from those who exhaust themselves chasing submissions from disadvantageous angles. The technique is most effective when the opponent retreats to a wide base or when fatigue begins compromising hip elevation, and it preserves offensive initiative by transitioning to a standing open guard rather than conceding position.

attacker.description: How to execute Technical Standup from Inversion in BJJ. Attacking perspective with setup, execution steps, and counters.
attacker.overview:
The Technical Standup from Inversion is a critical transitional skill that allows a inverted guard player to safely exit the inverted position and return to a standing open guard engagement. When the opponent disengages or creates too much distance for effective leg attacks from inverted guard, remaining inverted becomes a liability rather than an asset.
